content: Arcus senilis, also known by terms such as arcus corneae, arcus cornealis, arcus senilis corneae, arcus adiposus, or arcus juvenilis (when observed in younger individuals), is characterized by a white or gray opaque ring located at the peripheral margin of the cornea. This corneal opacity may be present at birth or develop later in life, becoming increasingly common in individuals over the age of 50. The condition arises due to cholesterol deposits or hyalinosis within the corneal stroma. It may be associated with ocular abnormalities or familial hyperlipidemia. When this condition occurs in younger individuals, it is referred to as arcus juvenilis. From a pathophysiological perspective, arcus senilis can serve as an indicator of lipid metabolism disturbances. It may signal underlying conditions such as hypercholesterolemia, hyperlipoproteinemia, or hyperlipidemia. Historically, arcus senilis was thought to be associated with atherosclerosis. However, findings from a large-scale, prospective, population-based cohort study (The Copenhagen City Heart Study) challenge this notion. This study followed 12,745 participants aged 20 to 93 years, all free of ischemic heart disease, over an average period of 22 years. Multivariate analyses, which adjusted for confounding factors such as cholesterol and triglyceride levels, demonstrated that arcus senilis is not an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic heart disease.
